messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 79
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:


Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raj Patel was seventy-nine years old, a retired warehouse worker, divorced for nearly two decades, and living alone in a small apartment on the outskirts of a Midwestern city. He had come to the clinic at the urging of his daughter, who had grown worried by how little he left the house, how he flinched when she knocked too loudly, and how he had stopped answering the phone for weeks at a time. Raj himself was not sure talking would help, but he was tired—tired of the weight in his chest, tired of the nights he spent sitting upright in the dark, waiting for something he could not name.

The thing that had happened to him was not something he spoke about. It had occurred in 1971, during his deployment as a young soldier in Vietnam. He had been part of a supply convoy that came under ambush near a village in the Central Highlands. The attack had been sudden, the noise deafening, and in the chaos he had watched the man beside him—a friend, a boy from California named Danny—take a round to the throat. Raj had tried to stop the bleeding, his hands slick and useless, while Danny made a sound that was not quite a scream and not quite a breath. The convoy had been pinned down for hours. By the time help arrived, Danny was gone, and Raj had sat in the mud with his friend’s blood drying on his arms, unable to speak. He had never told anyone the full story, not his wife, not his children. He had simply come home, gone to work, and tried to forget.

But the forgetting had not worked. Over the decades, the memory had not faded; it had only become more vivid, more intrusive. Now, in his small apartment, it would arrive without warning—the smell of damp earth and cordite, the sound of Danny’s ragged breathing, the weight of his body as Raj had tried to lift him. The memory was not like a story he told himself; it was like being pulled back into that moment, his heart hammering, his hands trembling, the present dissolving around him. He would find himself on the floor of his living room, unsure how he had gotten there, the television still playing some program he had not been watching.

He had come to believe that the world was not safe, that danger could appear at any moment from anywhere. This conviction had grown slowly, like a vine wrapping around his daily life. He stopped driving on highways because the sight of a bridge or an overpass made him feel trapped. He stopped going to the grocery store because the sudden sound of a dropped can or a child’s shout would send him spinning into a panic. He began to check the locks on his door three, four, five times before bed, and then again in the middle of the night. He was certain that if he let his guard down, something terrible would happen—not to him, necessarily, but to someone he cared about, and it would be his fault for not being vigilant.

The avoidance had become a kind of architecture for his life. He no longer attended family gatherings, claiming he was tired or unwell. He stopped calling his daughter, afraid that she would hear the tremor in his voice and ask questions he could not answer. He had not been to a doctor in years, not because he did not have aches and pains, but because the waiting room—the fluorescent lights, the muffled intercom, the strangers sitting too close—felt like a trap. His world had shrunk to the dimensions of his apartment, and even there, he could not rest. He kept the television on at all hours, not to watch, but to drown out the silence, because in the silence he could hear Danny’s voice, calling his name.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment that had shaken him more than usual. His daughter had come to visit and had brought her grandson, a boy of six who had run into the apartment laughing, his arms outstretched. The sudden motion, the high-pitched sound, had sent Raj into a flashback so intense that he had shoved the child away, hard, before he knew what he was doing. The boy had not been hurt, but he had cried, and Raj had seen the fear in his daughter’s eyes—not fear of him, but for him. She had not been angry. She had been sad. And that, somehow, was worse.

He sat now in the intake office, his hands resting on his knees, his gaze fixed on the floor. He did not know if he could tell the story. He did not know if he wanted to. But he was afraid, more than anything, of what he might do the next time he lost control. He was hoping, though he could not quite say it out loud, that someone might help him find a way to live without waiting for the ambush that had already happened to come again.
